hints: Think about the two gases involved in aerobic respiration in the peas - one is taken up and one is released. How would release of a gas affect the pressure change you are trying to measure?
walkthrough:
Link Gas Changes to Pressure**
Germinating peas respire aerobically, so they take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide. If both gases stayed in the test-tube air space, the pressure would hardly change and the coloured liquid would barely move.

Role of KOH**
Potassium hydroxide solution absorbs the carbon dioxide as soon as it is produced. That leaves only oxygen removal to lower the air pressure in the tube, which pulls the coloured liquid along. So the distance moved measures oxygen uptake and therefore rate of respiration.
Final answer: To absorb carbon dioxide produced by the germinating peas, so that movement of liquid is due only to oxygen uptake.

hints: Start by thinking what makes you trust a set of results - what would you do again at each temperature and what would you look for in the repeated values?
Now think about what else besides temperature could move the liquid, such as the peas themselves or changes in pressure. How could a second tube without living peas help you check this?
walkthrough:
Check Repeatability and Consistency**
Valid results should be reproducible. Repeat each temperature several times, then compare the repeats. Close, consistent values increase confidence. You can quantify spread with standard deviation or standard error, or use a statistical test.

Use a Control and Standardise Variables**
Set up a control respirometer identical in every way but with no respiration, for example glass beads of the same volume instead of peas. Any movement there is due to a fault such as a leak or atmospheric pressure change. Also check that other variables are kept constant, such as mass or volume of peas and volume or concentration of KOH.

Final answer: Repeat the investigation at each temperature and check consistency of results / calculate standard deviation or standard error; set up a control respirometer with non-living material e.g. glass beads instead of peas.

hints: Think about the temperature of the air and apparatus when first placed in the water-bath compared with five minutes later. Why would starting the timer at once give a misleading rate?
walkthrough:
Allow Time to Reach Target Temperature**
When the respirometer is first put in, the peas, air and KOH are still at room temperature. Leaving it for five minutes lets everything warm up or cool down to the water-bath temperature, so respiration is actually occurring at $10 ^\circ\text{C}$, $20 ^\circ\text{C}$ and so on when you start timing.
Final answer: To allow the apparatus and peas to acclimatise / equilibrate to the water-bath temperature before measurements begin.

hints: Look at Table 6.1 and Fig. 6.2 - temperature goes on the x-axis and rate on the y-axis. Check the scale carefully so each small square has a known value before placing any points.
Think about how to join the points for an enzyme-controlled rate that rises then falls - should it be straight ruler lines or one smooth curve through all the points?
walkthrough:
Plot Each Point Precisely**
Use temperature on the x-axis in $^\circ\text{C}$ and rate of movement in $\text{mm min}^{-1}$ on the y-axis. Plot carefully: 0.40 at 10, 0.70 at 20, 1.30 at 30, 1.15 at 40 and 0.60 at 50. Each small square is $0.02 \text{ mm min}^{-1}$ vertically, so count up accurately and mark a small neat cross.

Draw a Smooth Curve**
Join all points with a single smooth curved line, not straight ruler segments. The curve should rise to a peak near $30 ^\circ\text{C}$ then fall, passing through or very close to each point. Do not extend the line beyond the data.
Final answer: All 5 points plotted accurately at (10, 0.40), (20, 0.70), (30, 1.30), (40, 1.15), (50, 0.60); smooth curved line of best fit linking all plotted points, no extrapolation.

hints: Look at the trend in Table 6.1 - the rate rises from 0.40 to 1.30 between 10 and 30 degrees, then falls to 0.60 by 50 degrees. What type of biological molecules control respiration rate?
Think about what higher temperature does to molecular movement up to the peak. How would faster movement change how often enzymes and substrates meet?
Think about what happens to protein structure when it gets too hot past the peak. Why would the rate fall sharply after about 30 degrees?
walkthrough:
Respiration Depends on Enzymes**
Each step of respiration, including glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, is catalysed by enzymes. So the overall rate follows the pattern of enzyme activity with temperature.

Rising Limb - More Kinetic Energy**
From $10 ^\circ\text{C}$ to $30 ^\circ\text{C}$ the rate rises from $0.40$ to $1.30 \text{ mm min}^{-1}$. Molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so enzymes and substrates collide more often and a higher proportion of collisions have enough energy to react. More enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time, so oxygen uptake speeds up.

Falling Limb - Denaturation Past Optimum**
After about $30 ^\circ\text{C}$ the rate falls to $1.15$ then $0.60 \text{ mm min}^{-1}$. High temperature breaks bonds holding the enzyme in shape, the active site changes shape and enzymes denature. Fewer substrates fit, so rate drops. The peak near $30 ^\circ\text{C}$ is therefore the optimum temperature.

Final answer: Respiration is controlled by enzymes. As temperature rises to $30 ^\circ\text{C}$, kinetic energy increases, giving more frequent successful enzyme-substrate collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes, so rate increases. Above $30 ^\circ\text{C}$ enzymes denature with change in active site shape, so rate decreases; $30 ^\circ\text{C}$ is the optimum.
